title: How We Became Human
deck: Seven million years, a dozen kinds of human, and one that is left. Follow the fossils across the globe.
kidDeck: Once there were many kinds of humans. Follow the fossils to find out how we became the only ones left.

title: World War II
deck: The deadliest conflict in history, fought on every ocean and inhabited continent. Scroll through it day by day.
kidDeck: The biggest and most terrible war there has ever been. Scroll through it and see how it spread across the world, and how it ended.
contentNote: This story covers war, genocide, famine and the bombing of cities. It describes them plainly and without graphic images.

title: The Black Death
deck: In seven years a bacterium carried by fleas killed up to 50 million people. Follow it from port to port.
kidDeck: A tiny germ, carried by fleas, spread from town to town along the trade routes. Follow it across the map.
contentNote: This story describes a pandemic and the persecution that followed it.

title: The Silk Roads
deck: For sixteen centuries goods, gods and germs moved between China and the Mediterranean, one oasis at a time.
kidDeck: For 1,600 years, traders carried silk, paper and ideas between China and the West, from one desert town to the next.

title: The Mongol Empire
deck: In one lifetime a people of the steppe built the largest land empire in history. In another, it broke into four.
kidDeck: In one lifetime, horse riders from the grasslands built the biggest land empire ever. Watch it grow, and watch it split.

title: The Atlantic Slave Trade
deck: For more than three hundred years ships carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. This is the route, the people on it, and the people who ended it.
kidDeck: For more than 300 years, millions of African people were taken from their homes by force and shipped across the ocean. This is the story of that terrible trade, and of the people who fought to stop it.
contentNote: This story is about the enslavement of millions of people, and about those who resisted it. It includes deaths at sea and a massacre.

title: The Cold War
deck: Two superpowers, two blocs, and forty-four years in which they never fought each other directly. Visit the places where they nearly did.
kidDeck: For more than forty years two powerful countries were rivals. They never fought each other directly. Visit the places where things nearly went wrong.

title: The Columbian Exchange
deck: After 1492 two halves of the world that had been apart for thousands of years began trading plants, animals and germs. Nothing on your plate was ever the same.
kidDeck: After 1492, plants, animals and germs began crossing the Atlantic Ocean in both directions. It changed what the whole world eats.
contentNote: This story includes the deaths of most of the Indigenous population of the Americas from introduced diseases.

title: The day the dinosaurs died
deck: For more than 130 million years dinosaurs ruled the land. Then a rock ten kilometres wide fell out of the sky. Here is that day, and what the rocks remember of it.
kidDeck: Dinosaurs ruled the land for a very, very long time. Then a giant rock fell from space. Here is what happened that day, and how we found out.

title: Coal and the machine age
kidTitle: Coal and the age of machines
deck: A black rock made of ancient forests drained mines, smelted iron, drove engines and then changed the air. One link led to the next.
kidDeck: A black rock made from very old forests powered pumps, trains and factories. Each invention led to the next one. Follow the chain.

title: Out of the ground
deck: Ochre, flint, copper, tin, iron, silver, steel, lithium. Forty thousand years of digging, and what each new material made possible.
kidDeck: Red paint, sharp flint, copper, iron, silver, steel. People have been digging things out of the ground for 40,000 years. Each new material changed what they could make.

title: The story of nothing
deck: Ten small symbols, one of them standing for nothing at all, travelled from India to Baghdad to Italy and then into every computer on Earth.
kidDeck: The numbers you write every day were invented in India. The cleverest one is the one that means nothing: zero. Follow it around the world.

title: The printing press
deck: One workshop in Mainz in the 1450s. Presses in 236 European towns by 1500. Watch a machine for copying words spread across the map.
kidDeck: Before printing, every book was copied by hand. Then one workshop in Germany found a faster way. Watch the idea spread from town to town.

title: The spice routes
deck: Cloves grew on five small islands, nutmeg on a few more. For three and a half thousand years the world rearranged its sea lanes to reach them.
kidDeck: Cloves and nutmeg once grew on only a few tiny islands. People sailed across whole oceans to get them. Follow the spices from the islands to the kitchen.
contentNote: One scene of this story describes a massacre.

title: A day in Mohenjo-daro
deck: Forty thousand people, 4,500 years ago, with wells, drains and dice. Nobody can read a word they wrote. Walk through one day using only what was dug up.
kidDeck: 4,500 years ago, this was one of the biggest cities in the world. We cannot read its writing. But we can tell a lot about a day there from what people left behind.

title: Ibn Battuta: one life, 117,000 kilometres
deck: At 21 he left Tangier for Mecca, a trip of sixteen months. He came home 24 years later, by way of Kilwa, Delhi, the Maldives and China.
kidDeck: A young man set off from Morocco to visit Mecca. He kept going for almost thirty years, and travelled further than anyone before the age of engines.
